The contrast in MR images depends on three main parameters: the proton density, the longitudinal relaxation time T1, and the transverse relaxation time T2. These parameters can be adjusted by changing the time at which the signal is recorded, called echo time, and the interval between successive excitation pulses, called repetition time. A T1-weighted image is created by choosing a short repetition time, a T2-weighted image by choosing a long echo time, and a proton density (PD)-weighted image by minimizing both T1 and T2 weighting of the image (long repetition time and short echo time). The corresponding images are referred to as T1-weighted MRI, T2-weighted MRI, and PD-weighted MRI. Note that many variations of these sequences exist (for instance, gradient-echo vs spin-echo) and the corresponding implementation by different manufacturers usually comes with a specific commercial name (e.g., MPRAGE is a T1-weighted sequence available on Siemens scanners). Furthermore, many more anatomical sequences exist including T2*-weighted, T2-FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery), or DIR (double inversion recovery). Examples are displayed in Fig. 8. The set of sequences chosen by the radiologist will depend on the potential disease that is being investigated. Some examples in the context of machine learning are given in Subheading 23. steps.title: Organize Neuroimaging Data
steps.instruction: Organize data in folders and sub-folders on disk and name files according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specifications, including necessary metadata.

steps.title: Preprocess Anatomical MR Images
steps.instruction: Apply corrections to anatomical MR images to remove imperfections and ensure comparability across subjects.

substeps.instruction: Correct intensity inhomogeneities (bias field) using the N4 algorithm (available in ANTs).

Perform intensity normalization: globally rescale images (e.g., between 0 and 1), apply z-score normalization (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation), or use histogram matching for intensity standardization.
Perform brain extraction (skull stripping) to remove extracranial tissues using tools such as FSL or BrainSuite.
Spatially align images via medical image registration (rigid, affine, or nonrigid) using platforms like SPM, FSL, FreeSurfer, or ANTs.
Partition images into nonoverlapping regions (tissue types like gray/white matter or atlas-defined regions) via medical image segmentation.

steps.title: Preprocess Diffusion MR Images
steps.instruction: Correct artifacts in diffusion MR images before further analysis.

substeps.instruction: Correct magnetic susceptibility artifacts, eddy currents, intensity inhomogeneities, and subject movement using tools such as FSL or MRtrix.

steps.title: Preprocess Functional MR Images (fMRI)
steps.instruction: Limit nonneural variability and correct acquisition-related artifacts in fMRI data.

substeps.instruction: Perform susceptibility distortion correction.
Perform head motion correction by registering each volume in the time series to a reference volume.
Perform slice-timing correction to eliminate acquisition time differences between slices.
Perform physiologic noise correction via temporal filtering.
Use tools such as SPM, FSL, AFNI, or the fMRIPrep workflow.

steps.title: Preprocess CT Images
steps.instruction: Perform minimal preprocessing on CT images as required.

substeps.instruction: Extract the head from hardware elements (e.g., bed or pillow) or extract the brain using thresholding and morphological operators.
Perform spatial normalization.

steps.title: Preprocess PET Images
steps.instruction: Process PET images to allow for intersubject comparison and noise reduction.

substeps.instruction: Perform motion correction by rigidly registering each frame to a reference frame and averaging them into a single volume.
Perform intensity normalization to generate Standardized Uptake Value Ratios (SUVRs) by dividing the image by the mean uptake in a reference region.
Apply partial volume correction using tools such as PETPVC to limit activity spill-out.
Spatially normalize the image: rigidly register the PET image to an anatomical image (MRI or CT) and then to a template, or register the PET image directly to a PET template (e.g., via SPM).

steps.title: Preprocess SPECT Images
steps.instruction: Perform standard processing on reconstructed SPECT images.

substeps.instruction: Perform intensity normalization using a reference region.
Perform spatial normalization by registering the image to a SPECT template or first to an anatomical image.

steps.title: Extract Machine Learning Features
steps.instruction: Extract features based on the processed imaging modality and the desired analysis level.

substeps.instruction: Voxel-based features: Use raw intensities (deep learning), gray-level density, parametric maps (FA, MD for diffusion), or SUVR (PET/SPECT).
Vertex-based features: Extract cortical thickness and local surface area from surface meshes.
Regional features: Calculate volume or average image signal/SUVR within regions defined by an atlas.
Graph-based features: Construct networks where nodes are brain regions and edges encode connection strength (anatomical/functional) or network indices (efficiency, degree).
